The clay water pot outside the village school lay in pieces, and Hansa had been the last one near it.

"Did you knock it over?" asked Disha Madam.
"No, Madam." Hansa blinked, fast and hard, again and again.
"See, she's blinking. She's lying," whispered Bhola.

Disha Madam didn't answer him. She had seen Hansa blink like that every time she read aloud, and the dust storm that morning had left everyone's eyes red. "Blinking tells me you're nervous, Hansa, not what happened," she said. Then she asked the others. The tea-stall owner across the road had seen it: a grazing goat had butted the pot. Hansa's blinking slowed.

qa.q: What had knocked over the water pot?
qa.a: A grazing goat had butted the pot.

qa.q: What was Hansa most likely feeling as she blinked fast and hard?
qa.a: Nervous at being questioned about the broken pot. Her eyes may also have been sore from the dust storm, so the blinking showed stress or dust, not lying.

qa.q: Which choice was fair, and why?
qa.a: Disha Madam refused to treat blinking as proof and asked others who had seen, which found the real cause.

qa.q: How did Bhola read Hansa's blinking, and why was that unfair?
qa.a: Bhola took the blinking as a sign of lying, but blinking can come from nerves or dust, so it was no evidence at all.

grounding: It shows a child blinking a lot when nervous, a classmate reading it as lying, and a teacher treating it as nerves and checking the facts instead.

passage:
I'm Sangeeta, and in Class 5 I was sure Vikas hated me. Every time I stood at the board for my part of the group project, he narrowed his eyes at me like a cat about to pounce. I started mixing up my words.

One afternoon I finally asked him, "Why do you glare at me?"

He looked surprised. "I'm not glaring. The sun from that window hits the board, and I can't read anything. I squint at everyone."

A month later he came to school in glasses, and the "glare" disappeared. Now when someone narrows their eyes, I check where the light is before I decide they're cross.

qa.q: What did Vikas say hit the board?
qa.a: The sun from that window.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta feel when Vikas narrowed his eyes during the presentations?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt nervous and hurt, sure Vikas was angry, which is why the words got mixed up.

qa.q: What habit has Sangeeta taken from this?
qa.a: Checking the context, such as where the light is, before deciding someone is cross.

qa.q: What was it like for Vikas to be read as glaring?
qa.a: Vikas was just struggling to see the board and had no idea the squint looked angry, so the question came as a surprise.

grounding: It is a child's look back at reading a classmate's narrowed eyes as anger and learning it was squinting at a bright board.

subtype: Averting gaze when embarrassed or corrected [Expressing]
passage:
"Jatin, you skipped warm-up again." Coach Parveen's voice carried across the kabaddi mat.

Jatin stood still, eyes fixed on his toes, hands behind his back.

The new assistant coach, Mr Rego, stepped closer. "Look at the coach when she's talking. Don't be cheeky."

Jatin's ears went red, but his eyes stayed down.

Coach Parveen held up a hand. "Jatin, tell me what happened."
"Sorry, Coach. The bus was late, I came running. I didn't want to interrupt."

Later she told Mr Rego quietly, "His father once told me that at home, looking down at an elder means respect. And he was ashamed. It wasn't cheek."

qa.q: Why did Jatin say he missed warm-up?
qa.a: The bus was late, he came running, and he didn't want to interrupt.

qa.q: What was Jatin most likely feeling as he kept his eyes on his toes?
qa.a: Ashamed and embarrassed at being called out in front of everyone, as his reddening ears suggest; looking down may also be the respect he learned at home.

qa.q: What did Coach Parveen do that worked better than demanding eye contact?
qa.a: She asked Jatin what happened, which brought out the real reason, and later explained the lowered eyes to Mr Rego in private.

qa.q: Why might Mr Rego have read Jatin's lowered eyes differently?
qa.a: Mr Rego expects eye contact as a sign of listening, so lowered eyes looked like cheek; he didn't know what they meant in Jatin's family.

grounding: It shows a child looking away when corrected out of shame and learned respect, and a coach seeing it is not defiance.

subtype: Eye contact norms with elders in India [Mismatch]
passage:
In a Toronto classroom, Mr Diego Alvarez was asking who had spilled paint in the sink. Harsh, who had arrived from Pune two weeks earlier, answered, "Not me, sir," with his eyes on the teacher's shoes.

"Look at me when you say that," said Mr Alvarez.

Harsh lifted his eyes for one second, then dropped them again, his face hot.

After class Bao hung back. "Sir, Harsh isn't hiding anything. At his house you look down when an older person talks to you. My grandma taught me the same. Looking up would feel rude to him."

Mr Alvarez rubbed his chin. "And where I grew up, looking away meant lying. Maybe neither one means that."

qa.q: Where had Harsh arrived from?
qa.a: From Pune, two weeks earlier.

qa.q: What was Harsh likely feeling when he lifted his eyes for a second and dropped them again?
qa.a: He probably felt uncomfortable and embarrassed, caught between the teacher's request and the respect he learned at home; his hot face shows it.

qa.q: What could Mr Alvarez do next time a student avoids his eyes?
qa.a: Ask what happened and look at other facts, rather than treating eye contact, or its absence, as proof of honesty.

qa.q: How does Bao see the moment?
qa.a: Bao reads Harsh's lowered eyes as respect, from a similar upbringing, and is worried the teacher is taking them as lying.

grounding: It shows a child from an Indian family lowering his eyes to a teacher abroad, where eye contact is expected, and neither habit proving honesty or disrespect.

passage:
"Once more, Zainab. Write the seven times table again."
Zainab rolled her eyes to the ceiling and let out a long breath.
"I saw that," said Rukmini Ma'am.
"Saw what?"
"The eyes. Tell me what's wrong, in words."
"Nothing."
"Nothing doesn't roll its eyes."
Zainab's pen tapped the table. "It's the third time today. I know it already. And my hand hurts from school."
"Ah. So you're bored and tired, not being rude to me?"
"…Mostly."
Rukmini Ma'am smiled. "Fair. Say it aloud to me instead, fast as you can. Get it right and there's no more writing."
"Seven, fourteen, twenty-one…"

qa.q: Which times table was Zainab asked to write again?
qa.a: The seven times table.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling behind her eye roll?
qa.a: She felt bored and annoyed at writing the same table a third time, and tired from a sore hand; the roll let her show it without starting an argument.

qa.q: Which choice turned the eye roll into a better talk?
qa.a: Rukmini Ma'am calmly asked what was wrong in words instead of scolding, then changed the task to saying it aloud.

qa.q: How might Rukmini Ma'am feel when Zainab says "…Mostly"?
qa.a: She seems amused and understanding 🙂, taking the honest answer instead of treating the eye roll as an insult.

grounding: It shows a child rolling her eyes at a tutor out of boredom and annoyance, and a calm question opening a better talk than a scolding.

passage:
At the junior chess club in Dublin, Gabriel sat hunched over the board, cheeks sucked in, chewing the inside of one cheek. Across the table, Liam shifted in his chair. Every time Gabriel moved a knight, the face got tighter, as if he'd tasted something sour.

Liam put up his hand. "He's pulling faces at me. It's putting me off."

The club leader, Ms Byrne, crouched beside them. "Gabriel, are you doing that on purpose?"

Gabriel's cheeks popped out. He went pink. "Doing what? I always do that when I think. My mum says I'll chew a hole in my mouth."

Liam looked at the board, then at him, and almost laughed.

qa.q: What was Gabriel chewing while he thought?
qa.a: The inside of one cheek.

qa.q: Why did Liam put up his hand to complain?
qa.a: Liam felt uneasy and put off, reading Gabriel's tight, sour-looking face as a grimace aimed at him.

qa.q: What did Ms Byrne do that helped both boys?
qa.a: She asked Gabriel directly instead of scolding him, which showed the face was a thinking habit, not ill will.

qa.q: What is it like for Gabriel to learn his face was read as rude?
qa.a: Gabriel is surprised and embarrassed, since the cheek-chewing is just how he concentrates and calms himself.

grounding: It shows a child's drawn-in, chewed cheeks from concentration being misread as a grimace at an opponent, and a question clearing it up.

passage:
Lunch bell. Parul opened her steel tiffin: Amma's fish curry and rice, still warm. Beside her, Wasim wrinkled his nose and leaned away.

Parul's stomach dropped. She snapped the lid shut. Last year a girl had called her lunch "stinky", and the whole table had laughed. She sat with her hands in her lap for a long minute. Then she made herself ask, "Is it my food?"

Wasim looked confused. "Your food? No! Somebody left their football socks on the window ledge behind us. Can't you smell that?"

Parul sniffed. He was right. She opened the lid again, and Wasim asked if he could try a bite.

qa.q: What was in Parul's tiffin?
qa.a: Amma's fish curry and rice, still warm.

qa.q: Why did Parul snap the lid shut?
qa.a: She felt hurt and embarrassed, fearing Wasim was rejecting her food, because last year a girl had called her lunch "stinky" and everyone laughed.

qa.q: Which choice helped Parul avoid a wrong conclusion?
qa.a: She asked kindly, "Is it my food?", instead of assuming rejection, and found out it was the football socks.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel on learning Parul thought he disliked her lunch?
qa.a: He looks confused and probably a bit sorry, since he was only reacting to the socks; asking for a bite shows he wants her to feel okay.

grounding: It shows a child reading a friend's wrinkled nose as dislike of her lunch and asking kindly instead of assuming rejection.

subtype: Curling a lip and lip trembling in embarrassment [Mismatch]
passage:
The quiz at the Lajpat Nagar community hall came down to one question, and Aadhya buzzed first. "Correct!"

Mridul's upper lip curled. "Lucky guess," he said, loud enough for her team to hear. Aadhya's smile faded.

Then, as the clapping went on, Mridul's lip began to tremble. He pressed it hard between his teeth and stared at the buzzer, blinking.

Mr Bhasin, his teacher, didn't scold him in front of everyone. He said, "Mridul, help me carry the scoreboard," and walked him out to the corridor. There, away from the hall, Mridul burst out, "I practised every night for a month."

Mr Bhasin nodded. "I know. And you'll still need to say sorry to Aadhya."

qa.q: Where was the quiz held?
qa.a: At the Lajpat Nagar community hall.

qa.q: What might Mridul's curled lip and then his trembling lip show?
qa.a: First scorn and jealousy toward Aadhya, then a deep disappointment he was trying not to cry about in front of everyone, because he had practised so hard.

qa.q: How did Mr Bhasin protect Mridul's dignity while still dealing with the rude remark?
qa.a: He took Mridul out on an errand instead of scolding him publicly, listened to what lay behind it, and still asked for an apology to Aadhya.

qa.q: How might Aadhya feel on hearing "Lucky guess"?
qa.a: Her win is spoiled a little; she likely feels hurt and belittled, as her fading smile shows.

grounding: It shows a child curling a lip at a rival and then fighting a trembling lip in public, and a teacher protecting his dignity while looking at what led to it.

passage:
In the Class 6 classroom, Nandini sat on a small chair next to Papa while Mrs Rao flipped through her notebook. "Three science assignments missing."

Papa's lips pressed into a thin, flat line. He said nothing, just nodded. Nandini's fingers went cold. He's furious. He'll shout the whole way home.

In the corridor, she couldn't bear it. "Papa, are you very angry?"

Kishore stopped and rubbed his eyes. "A bit, about the science. But mostly I came straight from the night shift, and my head is pounding." He squeezed her shoulder. "We'll make a homework chart tomorrow. Tonight, I sleep."

Nandini let out her breath.

qa.q: How many science assignments were missing?
qa.a: Three science assignments were missing.

qa.q: What did Nandini think Papa's thin, flat lips meant?
qa.a: She read them as held-back fury and felt frightened, expecting shouting all the way home; her cold fingers show the fear.

qa.q: Why did Nandini's question work well?
qa.a: Asking calmly let Papa explain that he was only a bit annoyed and mostly exhausted from the night shift, so she didn't have to guess.

qa.q: What was going on for Kishore behind the tight lips?
qa.a: Kishore was a little annoyed about the science but mainly worn out and in pain after the night shift, holding it together in the meeting.

grounding: It shows a child reading a parent's tightened lips as held-back anger, and a calm question revealing it was partly anger and mostly tiredness.

passage:
Thursday

Today at swimming, Zeenat Aunty said, "Into the deep end, Urmila." I said NO. Aunty said my chin was sticking out "like an open drawer" and asked if I was being stubborn. She said, "You WILL get in," and I said, "I WON'T," and we just stood there glaring.

Then she did a strange thing. She sat down on the edge next to me and said, "Okay. Tell me why." I told her about last week, when I swallowed all that water and couldn't breathe for a second. My chin went back in by itself. She said we could do the deep end holding the rail today. I did it! Twice.

Urmila

qa.q: What did Zeenat Aunty say Urmila's chin looked like?
qa.a: Like an open drawer.

qa.q: What was Urmila really feeling behind the jutting chin?
qa.a: Fear: Urmila was scared of the deep end after swallowing so much water last week and wanted to be heard, not simply being stubborn.

qa.q: What went wrong first, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Aunty and Urmila got stuck in a "will" and "won't" power struggle; Aunty sitting down and asking why let the fear come out, and a smaller step, holding the rail, worked.

qa.q: How did Zeenat Aunty read the jutting chin at first?
qa.a: Zeenat Aunty took it as stubborn defiance, which is why the talk turned into a glaring match before she chose to listen.

grounding: It is a child's diary about a jutting jaw read as defiance that was really fear, and listening working better than a power struggle.
